CWE-15.name: External Control of System or Configuration Setting
CWE-15.question: Does this function let caller- or user-supplied input set a system or configuration setting without restriction?

any: input is passed to a setter for configuration, environment variables, database connection settings or system parameters
a key and value from a request are both used to change application settings
c: setenv, putenv, sysctl, setsockopt or a connection/catalogue setting call receives request-derived values
python: os.environ[...] = input, setattr(settings, key, value) or a connection option is set from request data
javascript: process.env[key] = value or config[key] = value uses request-derived key or value
rust: std::env::set_var or a config setter receives request-derived key or value

any: the key is checked against a fixed allow-list and the value is validated before the setting changes
the caller's authority to change the setting is checked first
the setting comes only from constants or trusted startup configuration

distinguish_from.CWE-73: the controlled value is a file path used in a filesystem operation

CWE-73.name: External Control of File Name or Path
CWE-73.question: Does this function pass a file name or path that comes from input or a caller into a filesystem operation?

any: request, argument, environment or file data reaches open, read, write, delete, rename, include or stat as all or part of a path
c: fopen, open, unlink, rename, stat or access receives a path built from input
cpp: std::ifstream, std::ofstream or std::filesystem::remove, rename or copy receives a path built from input
base / input with std::filesystem::path, where an absolute input replaces the base or ../ climbs out of it
python: open(), os.remove, shutil functions or pathlib operations use a path built from input
javascript: fs.readFile, fs.writeFile, fs.unlink, res.sendFile or require use a path built from input
rust: File::open, fs::read, fs::write or fs::remove_file use a path built from input

any: the path is a constant or is chosen from a fixed allow-list by key
the input is mapped to a server-generated name such as a database id or UUID
the resolved path is canonicalised and confirmed to stay inside an allowed base directory
cpp: std::filesystem::weakly_canonical of the joined path is confirmed to begin with the canonical base directory

distinguish_from.CWE-22: the input can climb out of an intended base directory with .. or absolute components
distinguish_from.CWE-15: the input sets a configuration value rather than a file path

CWE-134.name: Use of Externally-Controlled Format String
CWE-134.question: Does this function pass a format string that comes from input, a parameter or other non-literal source to a formatting function?

any: the format argument of a printf-style or template-formatting call is a variable derived from user input, a file, the network or the environment rather than a literal
c: printf(buf), fprintf(f, msg), sprintf(out, s), syslog(prio, s) or snprintf with a non-literal format and no "%s" in front
cpp: std::vformat, fmt::runtime or boost::format is given a format string taken from input
javascript: util.format or a logger's format method receives a user-supplied string as its first argument
python: user_text.format(...) or user_text % values, where the template itself is user-controlled and can reach attributes of the arguments

any: the format string is a literal and input is supplied only as an argument, such as printf("%s", s)
the input is only interpolated into a fixed template, never used as the template
c: the non-literal format comes from a fixed internal table of constant strings
cpp: std::format or fmt::format receives a literal format string, which is checked at compile time
rust: Rust format macros require a literal format string, so input cannot become the format

distinguish_from.REL-169: the concern is general use of stdio functions rather than an externally controlled format
distinguish_from.CWE-117: the input is written into a log unescaped but is not used as a format string

CWE-200.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
CWE-200.question: Does the function return, send, log, display or store data that could be sensitive, such as credentials, personal data, system details, errors or internal state?

any: responses, error messages, logs, debug output, files or URLs include secrets, personal data, stack traces, paths or configuration
behaviour or timing differs depending on secret values or whether an account or record exists
whole internal objects or records are serialised to an external party
the function handles only public or non-sensitive data and produces no output, logs or errors visible outside
the function performs internal computation with no external output channel

CWE-201.name: Insertion of Sensitive Information Into Sent Data
CWE-201.question: Does this function send data to another party (response, message, API call, email) that includes sensitive fields the recipient should not get?

any: a whole database record or internal object, including fields such as password hashes, tokens, keys or internal flags, is serialised into a response or outgoing message
secrets, session ids or other users' data are added to a payload, header, redirect URL or third-party request
javascript: res.json(user) or res.send(record) returns a full model object without picking or omitting sensitive fields
typescript: the declared return type is Omit<User, 'password'> or a narrower interface but the full object is returned; the type removes no fields at run time
a NestJS handler returns an entity whose password or token columns have no @Exclude() and no ClassSerializerInterceptor or DTO mapping
tsx: getServerSideProps, getStaticProps or a server component passes a full record with secrets to a client component, which serialises the props into the page
python: return jsonify(obj.__dict__) or a serializer with all fields sends a full model including secrets

any: only an explicit allow-list of non-sensitive fields is sent, or sensitive fields are removed first
the recipient is authorised for all the data sent, such as a user receiving their own non-secret profile
typescript: the entity is mapped field by field to a response DTO, or @Exclude() plus ClassSerializerInterceptor strips the sensitive fields

distinguish_from.CWE-598: the sensitive data is placed in the query string of an HTTP request
distinguish_from.CWE-209: the sensitive data reaches the recipient through an error message
distinguish_from.CWE-359: the sensitive data is personal information about individuals

CWE-203.name: Observable Discrepancy
CWE-203.question: Does this function respond, behave or take time differently depending on secret or security-relevant state, in a way an unauthorised caller can observe?

any: different messages, status codes or response shapes depending on whether a user, file or record exists or whether one part of a check failed
early return or branching on a secret value, so time taken reveals how much matched
a security check exits through visibly different paths, such as redirect versus error, depending on internal state
all failure cases return the same message, status and shape, and comparisons of secrets are constant-time
the differing information is public or the caller is already authorised to know it

distinguish_from.CWE-204: the difference is in the response content or status
distinguish_from.CWE-208: the difference is in how long the operation takes
distinguish_from.CWE-209: the response is an error message that directly includes sensitive details

CWE-204.name: Observable Response Discrepancy
CWE-204.question: Does this function return different messages, status codes or response content that reveal internal state, such as whether an account, file or record exists?

any: a login, reset or lookup returns one message for an unknown user and another for a wrong password or inactive account
status codes differ, such as 404 versus 403, in a way that reveals whether a protected resource exists
the response body or headers differ depending on a hidden check outcome that the caller should not learn
all failure outcomes produce the same message, status and response shape
the information revealed is public or the caller is authorised for it

distinguish_from.CWE-208: the observable difference is timing, while the response text is identical
distinguish_from.CWE-209: the message itself contains sensitive details rather than merely differing between cases

CWE-205.name: Observable Behavioral Discrepancy
CWE-205.question: Does this function behave in visibly different ways, such as extra steps, side effects or flows, depending on internal decisions an attacker should not learn?

any: a failed check triggers an observable action (lockout, extra request, redirect, delay) only in some hidden cases, revealing which internal condition held
processing stops at a visibly different stage depending on which internal validation failed
every failure follows the same observable flow and side effects
the differing behaviour reflects information that is public or that the caller is authorised for

distinguish_from.CWE-204: the difference is only in the response message or status code
distinguish_from.CWE-206: separate internal steps of one combined decision are each observable

CWE-206.name: Observable Internal Behavioral Discrepancy
CWE-206.question: Does this function make one combined security decision through separate steps whose individual outcomes an attacker can observe, such as checking username then password separately?

any: the function validates the parts of a credential or challenge one after another and returns or reacts at each step, so a caller can tell which part failed
an expensive step such as password hashing runs only after a cheaper check passes, so the outcome of the first check shows in behaviour or time
all parts are evaluated and a single combined result is returned with one uniform failure response
dummy work, such as hashing against a fixed value, is done when the first part fails so all paths look the same

distinguish_from.CWE-204: the steps are indistinguishable but the final response text differs
distinguish_from.CWE-1254: the steps are a byte-by-byte comparison of one secret value

CWE-207.name: Observable Behavioral Discrepancy With Equivalent Products
CWE-207.question: Does this function emit identifying details, such as product banners, version strings or distinctive headers or errors, that reveal which specific product or version is running?

any: a response, greeting banner or header includes a product name and version, such as Server or X-Powered-By values
error pages or protocol replies use distinctive non-standard text or ordering that identifies the implementation
responses use generic, standard-conforming text without product or version identifiers
version information is returned only to authenticated administrators or internal callers

distinguish_from.CWE-497: the exposed details are broader system information such as paths, users or environment

CWE-208.name: Observable Timing Discrepancy
CWE-208.question: Does this function take a measurably different time depending on secret data, such as comparing a secret with early exit or skipping work when a check fails?

any: a password, token, MAC or key is compared with ==, memcmp, strcmp, equals or a loop that stops at the first mismatch
a login or verification returns immediately for an unknown user but performs slow hashing for a known one
c: memcmp or strcmp compares a computed MAC or secret with an attacker-supplied value
cpp: std::string or std::vector operator==, compare() or std::equal on a MAC, token or password
javascript: a token or signature is compared with === instead of crypto.timingSafeEqual
python: a secret or HMAC is compared with == instead of hmac.compare_digest
rust: a secret slice is compared with == instead of a constant-time comparison such as subtle::ConstantTimeEq

any: secrets are compared with a constant-time function and all paths perform equivalent work
the compared values are not secret, such as public identifiers or enum values

distinguish_from.CWE-1254: the code shows a hand-written stepwise comparison loop that exits on the first differing element
distinguish_from.CWE-204: the response content differs rather than its timing

CWE-209.name: Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information
CWE-209.question: Does this function build or return an error message that includes sensitive details such as stack traces, queries, paths, credentials or internal state to the caller or user?

any: an exception's message, stack trace or repr is written into a response, UI or API error for external callers
error text includes SQL statements, file paths, host names, configuration, user records or secrets
javascript: res.status(500).send(err.stack) or res.json({error: err}) passes raw error objects to the client
typescript: a catch (e: any) or catch (e) block casts e as Error and returns e.message or e.stack to the client
python: return str(e) or traceback.format_exc() is placed in an HTTP response

any: external callers receive a generic message or error code, with details only logged internally
the error is shown only to a trusted operator, internal log or developer tool
typescript: an HttpException with a fixed message is thrown, and unknown errors reach the NestJS default filter, which replies with a generic 500

distinguish_from.CWE-210: the product composes the sensitive message itself
distinguish_from.CWE-211: the sensitive text comes from a library, runtime or interpreter error passed through
distinguish_from.CWE-532: the sensitive details go only to a log file

CWE-210.name: Self-generated Error Message Containing Sensitive Information
CWE-210.question: Does this function compose its own error or diagnostic message that embeds sensitive values, such as passwords, keys, queries, paths or user data, and show it to the caller?

any: an error string built by the function concatenates or interpolates a password, token, key, full query, file path or another user's data and is returned or displayed
a validation failure message echoes the secret or internal value that failed, such as 'invalid key abc123' or 'user x has role y'
the function's own messages are generic and include only non-sensitive context
detailed messages go only to an internal log or trusted operator, not to the external caller

distinguish_from.CWE-211: the sensitive text is generated by a library, runtime or interpreter rather than written by this code
distinguish_from.CWE-532: the self-made message is written only to a log

CWE-211.name: Externally-Generated Error Message Containing Sensitive Information
CWE-211.question: Does this function let an error produced by a library, runtime, database or interpreter reach the user with its original, possibly sensitive text?

any: a caught exception or driver error is returned or displayed unchanged, such as its message, stack or repr
an operation's failure is left uncaught in a request handler where the framework shows the raw runtime error
database or system call error text such as strerror or a SQL driver message is copied into the response
external errors are caught and replaced with a generic message before reaching the user
raw error text goes only to internal logs

distinguish_from.CWE-210: the message is written by the code itself rather than passed through
distinguish_from.CWE-535: the passed-through text is specifically shell command error output
distinguish_from.CWE-550: the exposure comes from a server or framework error page

CWE-213.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information Due to Incompatible Policies
CWE-213.question: Does this function deliberately reveal information that its users or data subjects would consider sensitive, such as other users' emails, locations or activity, as part of normal output?

any: a listing, search, profile or export returns fields about other users such as email, phone, IP address, location or history by design
the response includes data the feature does not need, such as precise location where a city would do
only data needed for the feature is returned, with sensitive fields omitted, masked or limited to the owner
the information is public by nature or consented to be shared

distinguish_from.CWE-359: the personal data is exposed because authorisation is missing rather than by intended design
distinguish_from.CWE-201: the extra data is accidentally included in a payload

CWE-214.name: Invocation of Process Using Visible Sensitive Information
CWE-214.question: Does this function start a process with passwords, keys or tokens in its command-line arguments or environment, where other local users could see them?

any: a child process is started with a secret passed as a command-line argument, such as -p<password> or --token=<value>
c: execv, execl, system or popen receives an argument or command string containing a password or key
javascript: child_process.spawn, exec or execFile is given args or an env containing passwords or tokens
python: subprocess.run, Popen or os.system is given a list or string containing a password or token
rust: Command::new(...).arg or .env receives a password, key or token

any: secrets are passed through standard input, a pipe, a file with restricted permissions or a credential helper
arguments and environment contain only non-sensitive values

distinguish_from.CWE-78: the concern is injection into the command rather than the visibility of its arguments
distinguish_from.CWE-532: the secret is written to a log rather than to process arguments

CWE-215.name: Insertion of Sensitive Information Into Debugging Code
CWE-215.question: Does this function contain debugging code, such as debug prints, dumps or debug-only endpoints, that outputs sensitive data like credentials, keys, tokens or personal details?

any: a debug print, trace, dump or console output includes passwords, tokens, keys, session ids or full request bodies
debug-only code that dumps sensitive state is enabled by a runtime flag, query parameter or left unconditional
c: printf or fprintf(stderr) inside #ifdef DEBUG or a debug flag prints secrets or buffers holding them
javascript: console.log or console.debug outputs passwords, tokens or full request headers
python: print(), pprint or logging.debug outputs credentials or secrets

any: debug output contains only non-sensitive diagnostic values
secrets are masked or redacted before any debug output

distinguish_from.CWE-532: sensitive data goes to a normal production log rather than debugging output
distinguish_from.CWE-1295: the debug message reveals system internals rather than user secrets

CWE-219.name: Storage of File with Sensitive Data Under Web Root
CWE-219.question: Does this function write sensitive data (credentials, keys, backups, logs, exports) into a directory the web server publishes as static content?

any: a file containing secrets, user records, database dumps or configuration is created under a path such as public/, static/, www/, htdocs/ or the web root
the output directory for a backup, export or log file is the application's served static folder
the file is written outside any served directory, such as a private data or temp directory
the content written is intentionally public, such as images, stylesheets or generated HTML pages
the function only reads or serves files and writes nothing sensitive

distinguish_from.CWE-433: the file written is raw source or an include file whose extension the server would return unparsed
distinguish_from.CWE-220: the destination is an FTP root rather than a web root

CWE-220.name: Storage of File With Sensitive Data Under FTP Root
CWE-220.question: Does this function write sensitive data into a directory served by an FTP server?

any: a file with secrets, user records, backups or configuration is created under a path that is the FTP root or an FTP-published folder
an export or upload routine targets an anonymous FTP or pub/ directory with private content
the destination is outside any FTP-published tree
the content written is intended for public download
the function writes no files

distinguish_from.CWE-219: the destination is a web document root rather than an FTP root

CWE-359.name: Exposure of Private Personal Information to an Unauthorized Actor
CWE-359.question: Does this function return or expose personal information about individuals, such as names with addresses, IDs, health or financial details, without checking that the requester is allowed to see it?

any: records containing personal data are fetched by an identifier from the request and returned without checking the requester owns them or has permission
personal details such as national ID, date of birth, address, health or financial data are sent, logged or displayed unmasked to parties who do not need them
an authorisation check ties the record to the requester or a permitted role before returning it
personal fields are removed, masked or aggregated before output
the data handled is not about identifiable people

distinguish_from.CWE-639: the code accesses records by a user-supplied key without an ownership check, whatever the data type
distinguish_from.CWE-532: the personal data is written to a log
distinguish_from.CWE-213: exposure is intended by the design but conflicts with users' expectations

CWE-374.name: Passing Mutable Objects to an Untrusted Method
CWE-374.question: Does this function pass a reference to its own mutable internal data to untrusted or external code, such as a callback, plugin or third-party API, without copying it first?

any: an internal array, list, map, buffer or object field is passed directly to a callback, plugin, listener or external library that could change it
the function relies on the passed data being unchanged after the call but did not copy it or pass a read-only view
typescript: an internal array or object is passed to a callback or plugin whose parameter is typed ReadonlyArray<T> or Readonly<T>; the callee can still mutate it at run time
c: a pointer to an internal buffer or struct, not const-qualified, is handed to a caller-supplied function pointer

any: a copy, clone or immutable view is passed instead of the internal object
the data passed is immutable, such as strings, numbers or frozen objects
the callee is trusted code in the same module and the function does not rely on the data staying unchanged
cpp: the parameter is passed as a const reference or by value
javascript: a spread copy, slice(), structuredClone or Object.freeze is applied before passing
python: a copy, tuple or frozenset is passed rather than the internal list, dict or set

distinguish_from.CWE-375: the internal mutable data is returned to the caller rather than passed out as an argument

CWE-375.name: Returning a Mutable Object to an Untrusted Caller
CWE-375.question: Does this function return a reference to its object's internal mutable data, such as a list, array, map or buffer, so callers can change internal state?

any: a getter or method returns an internal list, array, map, set or mutable object field directly rather than a copy
the returned object is security-relevant, such as a permission list, key buffer or configuration, that the class trusts afterwards
typescript: a method returns a private readonly array, Set or Map field itself, assuming the readonly modifier stops callers changing its contents
c: a function returns a non-const pointer to an internal static or struct buffer
cpp: a member function returns a non-const reference or pointer to a private container or member

any: a copy, clone or immutable view is returned
the returned value is immutable, such as a number, string or frozen object
returning a mutable reference is the intended contract and callers are trusted, such as a builder or internal helper
cpp: the return type is a const reference, by value or a span of const
javascript: a slice(), spread copy, structuredClone or Object.freeze result is returned
typescript: the method returns a copy, or wraps a copy in a ReadonlyArray<T> or ReadonlyMap return type
python: a copy, tuple, frozenset or MappingProxyType is returned

distinguish_from.CWE-374: the internal data is passed as an argument to untrusted code rather than returned
distinguish_from.CWE-495: the returned reference is to a private data structure in a class, which is the more precise entry

CWE-377.name: Insecure Temporary File
CWE-377.question: Does this function create or use a temporary file in an unsafe way, such as a predictable name, a shared directory, a create-after-check race or loose permissions?

any: a temporary file name is generated first and the file opened later, or a fixed or guessable name in a shared temp directory is used
a temp file is opened without exclusive creation, so an existing file or symlink could be reused
c: tmpnam, tempnam or mktemp is used, or fopen opens a fixed path under /tmp
cpp: std::tmpnam, or std::filesystem::temp_directory_path() / a fixed name, opened with std::ofstream
javascript: fs.writeFile or fs.open writes to path.join(os.tmpdir(), fixedOrPredictableName)
python: tempfile.mktemp or open('/tmp/name', 'w') is used instead of mkstemp, NamedTemporaryFile or TemporaryDirectory
rust: std::env::temp_dir().join(fixed_name) is opened with File::create rather than using the tempfile crate or create_new

any: the file is created atomically with a random name and exclusive creation, such as mkstemp, tmpfile, tempfile.mkstemp or the tempfile crate
the temp file lives in a private directory created with owner-only permissions
cpp: the file comes from mkstemp and the stream is attached to that descriptor, or it sits in a private directory

distinguish_from.CWE-378: the file is created safely but with permissions that let others read or write it
distinguish_from.CWE-379: the problem is the directory chosen being accessible to other users
distinguish_from.CWE-367: the defect is a check-then-use race on a file that is not specifically temporary

CWE-378.name: Creation of Temporary File With Insecure Permissions
CWE-378.question: Does this function create a temporary file with permissions that let other users read or modify it?

any: a temporary file is created with a mode such as 0644, 0666 or 0777, or with the default umask, and holds data other users should not see or change
c: open(path, O_CREAT, 0666) or fopen is used for a temp file without first setting a restrictive umask
cpp: std::ofstream creates the temp file, so it gets the default 0666 mode reduced only by the umask
javascript: fs.writeFileSync or fs.openSync creates a temp file with mode 0o666 or no mode option
python: os.open with mode 0o644 or wider, or os.chmod widening a temp file's permissions
rust: OpenOptions creates a temp file with mode(0o644) or broader, or without setting mode on Unix

any: the temp file is created with owner-only permissions, as mkstemp, tempfile.mkstemp, NamedTemporaryFile and the Rust tempfile crate do by default
the file holds only public, non-sensitive data and is not used for later decisions

distinguish_from.CWE-377: the main flaw is a predictable name or unsafe creation sequence rather than the permissions
distinguish_from.CWE-379: the file itself is restrictive but sits in a directory others can access

CWE-379.name: Creation of Temporary File in Directory with Insecure Permissions
CWE-379.question: Does this function create a temporary file in a directory that other users can list or write, such as a shared /tmp or a world-writable folder, where its presence or name can be seen or abused?

any: a temp file holding sensitive data is created directly in a shared system temp directory rather than a private per-user subdirectory
the function creates a temp directory with permissive modes such as 0777 and places files in it
c: mkdir with mode 0777 or chmod widening a temp directory before files are written into it
javascript: fs.mkdirSync with mode 0o777 or files written into os.tmpdir() with names revealing the application or user
python: os.makedirs(..., mode=0o777) or files written straight into /tmp or tempfile.gettempdir() with descriptive names
rust: create_dir with permissions 0o777, or files written straight into the shared temp_dir() with descriptive names

any: a private temp directory is created with owner-only permissions, such as mkdtemp or tempfile.TemporaryDirectory, and files go inside it
the temp file holds no sensitive data and its name reveals nothing

distinguish_from.CWE-378: the file itself is created with weak permissions
distinguish_from.CWE-377: the flaw is the naming or creation method rather than the directory

CWE-402.name: Transmission of Private Resources into a New Sphere ('Resource Leak')
CWE-402.question: Does this function hand a private resource, such as a descriptor, handle, memory, credential or connection, to a less trusted process, party or sphere?

any: open descriptors, sockets or handles remain inheritable when the function starts a child process or hands control to other code
an internal handle, connection object or key is passed to plugins, scripts or clients that should not use it
c: fork or exec is called while sensitive descriptors are open without FD_CLOEXEC or O_CLOEXEC

any: resources are closed, marked non-inheritable or kept private before control passes to less trusted code
the receiving process or party is equally trusted and meant to have the resource
rust: only std::process::Command is used, which marks descriptors close-on-exec by default

distinguish_from.CWE-403: the leaked resource is specifically a file descriptor inherited by a child process

CWE-403.name: Exposure of File Descriptor to Unintended Control Sphere ('File Descriptor Leak')
CWE-403.question: Does this function start a child process while sensitive file descriptors or handles are still open and inheritable?

any: a privileged file, socket or device is opened and still open when the function starts a child process, without being closed or marked non-inheritable
c: open, socket or fopen without O_CLOEXEC or FD_CLOEXEC, followed by fork and exec, system or popen
javascript: child_process.spawn is called with stdio including open file descriptors from the parent
python: subprocess.Popen(..., close_fds=False) or pass_fds includes sensitive descriptors, or os.set_inheritable(fd, True) is used
rust: unsafe pre_exec code or libc fork and exec keep sensitive descriptors open in the child

any: descriptors are opened with close-on-exec or closed before the child starts
the child is meant to receive the descriptor and is equally trusted
python: Popen is used with its default close_fds=True and no pass_fds
rust: only std::process::Command is used, which marks descriptors close-on-exec by default

distinguish_from.CWE-402: the leaked resource is something other than a descriptor

CWE-426.name: Untrusted Search Path
CWE-426.question: Does this function load a program, library or resource by searching a path list that untrusted input or the environment can influence?

any: a library, plugin, module or executable is located through PATH, LD_LIBRARY_PATH, PYTHONPATH, NODE_PATH or a search list built from input
c: execlp, execvp, system or popen run a command by bare name, or dlopen/LoadLibrary is given a bare or relative name
python: sys.path is extended from input, or subprocess runs a bare command name with an env taken from the caller
javascript: require or child_process uses a bare name while module or PATH directories come from input
rust: Command::new with a bare name runs while PATH is taken from input, or libloading opens a relative name

any: programs and libraries are referenced by absolute, fixed paths
the search path is reset to a fixed safe value before the lookup
the name and directories involved are constants and nothing in the function lets input change them

distinguish_from.CWE-73: input supplies the file path directly rather than the search path
distinguish_from.CWE-427: the search path includes an uncontrolled element such as the current directory

CWE-427.name: Uncontrolled Search Path Element
CWE-427.question: Does this function load executables, libraries, modules or config files through a search path that includes locations untrusted users could control?

any: a library, module or program is loaded by bare name or relative path, so the current directory or a writable path is searched
the function adds the current directory, /tmp, a user-writable or input-supplied directory to PATH, LD_LIBRARY_PATH, sys.path or a module path
c: dlopen or LoadLibrary with a bare file name, or execlp or execvp in a privileged program with PATH not reset
javascript: require or import of a path built from input or a writable directory, or NODE_PATH or PATH is extended with such a folder
python: sys.path.insert(0, writable_or_input_dir), or importlib loads a module from a user-writable location
rust: libloading Library::new with a bare name, or Command::new with a bare program name after PATH was changed to include a writable directory

any: libraries and programs are loaded by absolute path from trusted, admin-only directories
the search path is reset to a fixed safe list before loading
the loader restricts searching to system directories, such as LoadLibraryEx with system-only search flags

distinguish_from.CWE-426: the whole search path is supplied by an attacker rather than one element being writable
distinguish_from.CWE-428: the problem is an unquoted path containing spaces

CWE-428.name: Unquoted Search Path or Element
CWE-428.question: Does this function build or run a command or service path containing spaces without quoting it, so a different program higher in the path could be run?

any: a program path with spaces, such as C:\Program Files\App\app.exe, is passed unquoted as a command line
a service, registry or shortcut path is written without surrounding quotes
c: CreateProcess with a NULL application name and an unquoted command line containing spaces, or WinExec with such a path
javascript: child_process.exec with an unquoted path containing spaces
python: subprocess with shell=True or os.system given an unquoted path containing spaces

CWE-433.name: Unparsed Raw Web Content Delivery

CWE-493.name: Critical Public Variable Without Final Modifier
CWE-493.question: Does this function create or expose a security-critical field as public and mutable, so any code can overwrite it, such as a role, limit or configuration value?

CWE-497.name: Exposure of Sensitive System Information to an Unauthorized Control Sphere

CWE-498.name: Cloneable Class Containing Sensitive Information

CWE-500.name: Public Static Field Not Marked Final

CWE-524.name: Use of Cache Containing Sensitive Information

CWE-525.name: Use of Web Browser Cache Containing Sensitive Information
CWE-525.question: Does this web handler return sensitive pages or data without headers that stop the browser or proxies from caching them?

javascript: res.send or res.json of authenticated content with no res.set('Cache-Control', 'no-store'), or caching middleware applied to private routes
python: a view returns sensitive data without the framework's never-cache helper or a no-store Cache-Control header

any: no-store or private, no-cache headers are set on the response, here or by middleware the function visibly applies

distinguish_from.CWE-539: the sensitive data is kept in a persistent cookie

CWE-532.name: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File
CWE-532.question: Does this function write sensitive information, such as passwords, tokens, keys, session ids or personal data, to a log?

distinguish_from.CWE-215: the output is debugging code rather than the production log

CWE-535.name: Exposure of Information Through Shell Error Message
CWE-535.question: Does this function run a shell or system command and return or display its error output, such as stderr or exit messages, to the user?

CWE-538.name: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Externally-Accessible File or Directory

python: open(...).write saves secrets into a static, media or shared directory, or the mode is not restricted

distinguish_from.CWE-312: the core issue is storing the secret unencrypted, wherever it is stored

CWE-539.name: Use of Persistent Cookies Containing Sensitive Information

CWE-541.name: Inclusion of Sensitive Information in an Include File

CWE-548.name: Exposure of Information Through Directory Listing

CWE-615.name: Inclusion of Sensitive Information in Source Code Comments
